item.title: The Overhead Lighting Debate
item.description:
Good morning! Do you prefer overhead lighting or more ambient lighting?

Some people are making their answer a part of their personality. Personally, I’m an ambient guy. My sensitive eyes can’t handle the harshness of overhead lights. Mariah Carey agrees with me. Convince me I’m wrong.

We’re also covering:

Student protests

Fiona the hippo

The G.T.A. flu

What to discuss in class today.

1. The Senate passed a bill that would speed up energy projects. It represents the biggest change to environmental law in a generation, experts said. The legislation would overhaul federal permitting laws to build everything from gas pipelines to wind farms. It faces an uncertain future in the House.

2. Students are protesting across Europe today. Thousands of students are expected to demonstrate, following France’s lead. It’s the latest example of global youth anger.

3. Many Anthropic employees became millionaires overnight. Some who joined the company a few years ago are now worth tens of millions of dollars, if not more, after its record-setting initial public offering.

4. Jensen Huang made humiliation a routine at Nvidia. His belittling behavior toward employees goes back decades, and his insults were savage. Read them here.

5. Fiona, an internet-famous hippo, has died. She became sick after she ate a children’s knit hat that accidentally fell into her enclosure. She was 9.

Your questions about the news, and life, answered.

What’s going on with the duration of status (D/S) policy, and what does it mean for an international student? Is it safe for international students to go home for break? — Luna Kwon, 23, theater major at Wesleyan University

Thanks for the question, Luna. I asked Miriam Jordan, who covers immigration, to tackle this one:

Duration of Status (D/S) allows international students to remain in the U.S. for the time necessary to complete their studies or training, which sometimes takes longer than expected. The Trump administration recently tried to replace it with a fixed period. This would have required a student needing more time to obtain their degree to request an extension. It would also have limited school transfers, major changes and other program alterations. A federal court struck down the rule in November, preventing it from going into effect. “Duration of Status” doesn’t have any impact on the ability to enter or re-enter the country after travel.The question of whether it is safe to travel outside the U.S. is a very individual one, experts said. They suggest international students consult with a designated official at their institution before making plans to travel outside the U.S.

Submit your questions to Office Hours.

Deion Sanders, the head coach of the University of Colorado Boulder’s football team, has said that he regularly receives death threats. The Athletic obtained police records about the harassment.

The number of new Ph.D. students studying the sciences (including engineering and mathematics) at major research institutions dropped 10 percent during the first year of President Trump’s second term.

The Justice Department charged a former fraternity brother at Penn State University who prosecutors said was a major supplier of cocaine to fraternities. (NBC News)

The president of Tufts University emailed an apology to the school acknowledging the school’s failure to support a student who said in an anonymous opinion essay that she was sexually assaulted. (The Tufts Daily)

A new movie from the “Hunger Games” franchise is out. I caught an early screening of “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” with my friends. The reviews have been mixed. (And the red carpet looks from the press tour have been intense.)

Did you have the G.T.A. flu? Some schools and businesses were bracing for people to call in sick after the highly anticipated game dropped. But some of you emailed me and said you didn’t skip class!

A “Saturday Night Live” sketch went viral. Watch it here.

Do this to get ahead.

A.I. has changed the way we talk. If you’re confused about all the terms, my colleague created a helpful glossary with all the words you need to know.

Avoid these foods. Some food safety experts say they aren’t worth the risk.

Dust off those winter boots. Only if it’s getting cold, of course. Need a new pair? Me too. Here are the best ones.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you next week!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

Lauren Jackson edited Extra Credit today. Harrison Hill and Scott Ball were our photo editors.

item.title: A New Era of A.I.-Driven Chaos? That Might Just Be Progress.
item.description:
A nationwide ground stop on all flights. Customers unable to conduct transactions at America’s largest bank. Microsoft Outlook down. Apple services inaccessible. Even, the National Security Agency’s classified email system went offline.

A spate of recent tech outages and the resulting mayhem annoyed and puzzled many people. Some officials linked the outages to routine tech upgrades. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, suggested that a cause might be the global rush to build defenses against A.I. hackers, although no public evidence suggested cyberattacks had caused any of the failures.

Such mishaps may seem like unique crises of the information age. But historians of technology call them mundane. They argue that disasters in complex systems are inevitable parts of innovation’s boom-bust cycles. In ages past, the advancements often came with the loss of thousands of lives, such as steamboat explosions at the dawn of the industrial age. There was also the Hindenburg disaster in the early years of commercial flight and the Apollo 1 fire near the start of the space age.

From this view, the recent outages are simply part of the learning curve, and blessedly bloodless. Because inventors tend to work at the cutting edge of physics, materials science and human understanding, significant failures — trial and error — are the main way they uncover the hidden flaws behind their bright ideas.

Historians tend to agree that the cycles of progress and failure have been part and parcel in the creation of steam power, electrical grids, airplanes, chemicals, medicine, rocketry and computers.

Charles Perrow, a Yale sociologist best known for his 1984 book, “Normal Accidents: Living With High-Risk Technologies,” said that major failures in complex systems were not just probable but unavoidable, regardless of the level of competency in a system’s management, safety training and prevention steps.

And Henry Petroski, a Duke University historian, put a positive spin on a similar argument, writing that failure was a prerequisite for breakthroughs.

The high-pressure steam boilers of the 19th century regularly exploded. On steamboats plying American rivers, the violent bursts killed thousands of people before public rules emerged for passenger safety, pressure-relief valves and standardized steel alloys. In 1865, a blast near Memphis killed 1,700 passengers, many of them discharged Union prisoners.

So, too, early electrical wiring led to calamitous urban fires, and linemen were frequently electrocuted on live overhead wires. The tragedies led to better insulation, circuit breakers and wire grounding that redirected stray currents.

Early airplanes experienced structural failures, engine stalls and aerodynamic riddles that baffled pilots. The de Havilland Comet, the world’s first commercial jetliner, had a series of fatal breakups starting in 1953. In time, engineers found that the square shape of the plane’s windows caused nearby structures to crack and weaken to the point that the plane’s body would rupture.

Drugs and industrial chemicals were made public without clinical trials or toxicology screening. Things like radium, lead paint and early synthetic drugs caused severe harm before the establishment of regulatory frameworks and bodies, such as the Food and Drug Administration.

Rocketry and spaceflight were dazzling spectacles of catastrophic failure. In 1957, the Atlas, America’s first intercontinental ballistic missile, roared off the launchpad on its inaugural flight test. It lasted 24 seconds before the engines failed.

All these nascent technologies managed, on balance, to turn the corner and make the world a better place, where safety tends to rule and people tend to prosper.

It took years and sometimes decades of detective work, tinkering, public protests, lawsuits, building codes, safety margins, tech standards and independent bodies that certify safety — all on top of engineers and designers learning as much as they possibly could from the lessons of failure.

Most often, catastrophic failures in the past were caused by the limits of what was known, or could be known, without first trying. But in some instances, they were the result of recklessness, born from a desire to be first, or faster or cheaper.

That recklessness can be tempered, said Ryan Hearty, a historian of technology at Johns Hopkins University, who rejects the idea that failures are inevitable.

The dangers “can be managed with safety in mind,” he said. The objective, he added, is to “‘move slow and upgrade’ instead of ‘move fast and break things’” — a tech-industry motto popularized by Mark Zuckerberg at Facebook.

Political factors, some analysts said, can intensify or lessen the cycles of technological feats and failures.

“We’ve invested a great deal of money in large, complex systems that we don’t completely have a handle on,” said Matthew Hersch, a historian of technology at the Institute for Advanced Study at Princeton.

Often making matters worse is the fact that those systems are not properly maintained. In the case of the recent F.A.A. outage, officials blamed the running of new software on old copper wiring. That infrastructure had not been upgraded because of spending cuts.

“What we’re seeing now,” Dr. Hersch said, “is a collapse of infrastructure due to neglect, as a result of penny-pinching.”

“It’s not sexy,” he added, pointing to upkeep on air traffic control systems and power grids. “We know exactly how to fix them. It’s about money, and the money hasn’t been spent.”

The frenetic pace of A.I. tends to intensify the alarms, risk analysts say. Modern society is already hooked on devices that rely on advanced semiconductors and is quickly becoming reliant on artificial intelligence.

“We don’t recognize how dependent we are on certain systems until they stop working,” said Zachary Loeb, a historian of technology at Purdue University. “And it’s easy to assume that things will keep working because, generally, they do.”

But there is hope that proactive measures can help insulate us from catastrophe.

A case study is Y2K — or the millennium bug, a threat that arose as the calendar turned to the year 2000. To save memory, computers had been programmed to read years as two digits rather than four, as in “99” for “1999.”

People feared that banks, power grids, air traffic control, elevators and medical devices would shut down. However, a major global effort rewrote millions of lines of computer code, making the new millennium largely uneventful.

“There was this laserlike focus,” Dr. Loeb said. The moral, he added, is never “to take things like computers and electricity for granted.”

item.title: The Anti-A.I. Campus Movement Is Growing
item.description:
Last March, a handful of students at Transylvania University created a petition, attempting to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus. It asked the administration to cancel chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and instead invest the money in “human-centered education.”

About a third of the college’s students signed on.

Transylvania, in Lexington, Ky., is tiny, with under 1,000 students. But across the country and the globe, there has been a swell of campus resistance to A.I., including a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all.

Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work. College leaders have generally embraced A.I., saying it is key to preparing students for the work force.

But as A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down.

Much of the opposition comes from the political left, and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices in opposition are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.

But there are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself, by removing the productive struggle of learning.

Resistors from California to Sydney to Paris are increasingly publishing manifestoes that lay out demands: that colleges not partner with A.I. companies; that professors not be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading; and that students be allowed to refuse to complete assignments that require the use of chatbots, without any impact on their grades.

At the University of Kentucky, a research employee who described himself as a humanist successfully applied for a religious exemption from using A.I.

Alice Beatty, 22, helped lead the Transylvania petition drive as a senior last spring. The student newspaper had called attention to the $120,000 the university paid to purchase licenses to ChatGPT and Gemini, chatbots from OpenAI and Google. And Ms. Beatty had participated in a discussion group formed by several A.I.-skeptical professors.

She noted that even before Transylvania provided free access to chatbots, A.I. had been everywhere on campus. Students used it to summarize readings, break down physics problems and compose discussion-board posts and papers that they were supposed to be writing the old-fashioned way, on their own.

Yet when Ms. Beatty and some classmates stood near the dining hall to collect signatures on the petition, almost everyone they spoke to signed.

“I use A.I.,” she recalled some peers telling her, “and I am ashamed I use it.”

A spokeswoman for Transylvania University declined an interview request but said that professors were free to either embrace A.I., limit its use or ban it entirely in their classes.

For students, ethical and practical questions about A.I. will be part of the world they enter after graduating, she said by email.

Vague and confusing college A.I. policies have helped create the conscientious objector movement, said Hollis Robbins, an English professor at the University of Utah who writes often about A.I. and education. She suggested that colleges stop grading take-home assignments that are easy to cheat on with A.I., and shut down online courses that have become rife with academic misconduct in the A.I. era.

If institutions took those steps, she argued, students might be more curious and hopeful about the technology.

“There is silence about these major tech issues,” she said. “Students just seeing grown-ups being inconsistent and letting them down.”

Georgetown University began offering students and faculty free access to Gemini in March. At the time, like many institutions, Georgetown generally allowed each professor to set their own A.I. rules.

Yet in focus groups on A.I. conducted by the university, students asked for clearer guidance. They were worried about cognitive offloading, cheating and A.I. providing false information. Forty percent of the student sentiment was cautious or negative toward A.I., according to the university, compared with 25 percent that was positive or hopeful.

Georgetown’s student newspaper published an editorial criticizing the Gemini license, arguing that it tacitly pushed students toward technology that is often used to plagiarize and avoid academic effort.

This fall, the university is changing its approach. Under a new president, Eduardo M. Peñalver, it announced it would form a faculty committee to come up with clearer principles on A.I. use. For Georgetown, a Jesuit institution, Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical on the risks of A.I. will be an important influence.

Dr. Peñalver said in an interview that Georgetown would seek to make course expectations around A.I. more transparent and provide more tech-free spaces on campus. Oral presentations, discussion groups and in-person tests would become more important, he said, to protect “from the intrusion of this technology.”

Still, the university will continue to expand free access to A.I. tools, which he said had the potential to do good.

“We’re not interested in pushing people to use A.I. in ways that don’t align with their values,” Dr. Peñalver said. “But I certainly encourage people to learn about it.”

“Even if you’re opposed to this technology,” he added, “that awareness and understanding is important to the success of your project.”

Many conscientious objectors, though, say they try to avoid generative A.I. as much as possible, blocking it from their devices and not experimenting with it in their own work.

Emily Tucker, executive director of the Center on Privacy and Technology at Georgetown Law School, has been a leader in organizing resistance to A.I. use on campus. She has also signed an open letter with 1,300 other educators “who refuse the call for generative A.I. adoption in schools and colleges, and reject the narrative of its inevitability.”

Law students have told her they feared that if they didn’t use A.I. to speed their output, they would be outpaced in class and at work by those who did. But Professor Tucker said that using A.I. degrades a student’s ability to read and analyze dense legal texts, and risks incorrect citations of case law.

“It’s not useful,” said Professor Tucker, who said she rarely uses A.I. herself, though she acknowledged it might help in some tasks, like seeking specific information within a large set of documents.

At Cornell, Shimon Edelman, a psychology professor who holds a Ph.D. in computer science, has also signed the anti-A.I. letter. He lets students decide whether or not to use A.I., though he warns them it could degrade deeper learning.

He said he had been dismayed to see the Cornell administration greet A.I. warmly, as an “essential tool,” instead of warning more forcefully against its risks. In October, Cornell announced free access to chatbots, A.I. coding tools and agentic A.I.

“It’s unthinkable,” Professor Edelman said of using A.I. in his own research, even when he faced having to read 800 documents for a recent book project.

Emmali Simmelink, a senior studying classics and religion at Whitman College in Washington State, said students on her campus sometimes plug classroom discussion prompts directly into ChatGPT.

“If you can’t generate a coherent thought without ChatGPT, I genuinely lose a lot of respect for you,” she said. She added, laughing, “I am really insufferable about this.”

She said she brings up concerns about the environmental impact of A.I. as soon as she hears somebody say, “I asked ChatGPT.”

The topic can be divisive socially, so much so, several students said, that friend groups often develop a shared view of A.I.

Preston Hicks, 26, is studying history and education at Rider University in New Jersey — a second degree, after he worked previously as a software developer. He said many of his friends are artists who instinctually oppose A.I., a view he often shares.

But he can also imagine using A.I. in his future career as a teacher, to handle paperwork and other logistical tasks.

“I am more nuanced,” he said. “If I see a good use, I will use it.”

item.title: New Ph.D. Enrollment in the Sciences Dropped 10 Percent Under Trump
item.description:
The number of new Ph.D. students studying science, engineering, health, mathematics and computer science at major research institutions in the United States fell substantially during the first year of President Trump’s second term, according to a new federal survey.

The decline, about as steep as what occurred during the Covid-19 pandemic, was largely — but not entirely — driven by a drop in international students. It indicates that schools are pulling back on research in a range of fields amid the turbulence in higher education.

First-time doctoral students at 187 top research schools

Source: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

According to an analysis of the survey data by The New York Times, the overall number of new full-time doctoral students in the surveyed fields at the nation’s 187 top research schools fell by about 5,100 in 2025. That number represented a decline of 11 percent from the prior school year. A similar trend held across the survey’s broader set of schools, which saw a decline of 10 percent.

Plummeting enrollment among international students accounted for nearly three-quarters of the drop at the top research schools, a sign that those students may have been dissuaded from studying in the United States by the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrants and efforts to limit visa stays.

A White House report released over the summer, which committed to initiating a “new golden age” of American science, described an “overreliance” on international talent as an issue of national security. “The United States has funded large cohorts of foreign students and tolerated technology transfer abroad under lax security standards,” the report read. “This reliance on foreign talent sidelines American students, a deep domestic talent pool that remains undersupported by its own government.”

But according to the survey data, the number of U.S. citizens and permanent residents enrolling in full-time doctoral programs also dropped. At top research schools, 1,450 fewer of these students enrolled in 2025 than in the previous year.

Funds that support doctoral research have been disrupted as the federal government cut or threatened grant money, agencies lost staff and the Trump administration shifted to new priorities.

The total number of full-time doctoral students remained essentially flat. But the declines are the first time that new enrollments have fallen since 2020, when they dropped due to pandemic restrictions before rising again in 2021 as those restrictions eased.

The data does not capture any changes this school year, but information collected from a group of major research schools shows even steeper declines among doctoral enrollments this fall.

“Graduate students are both today’s and tomorrow’s scientific work force, and a sustained decline in doctoral enrollments could affect research capacity for years to come,” said Travis York, a director at the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “It’s the people entering doctoral programs today that will lead discoveries in biotechnology, computing, energy, engineering, A.I. and other fields over the next decade.”

The new figures come from an annual survey by the National Science Foundation of institutions across the United States that offer graduate degrees in science, engineering or health programs. Known as the Survey of Graduate Students and Postdoctorates in Science and Engineering, the findings offer broad insight into enrollment and completion trends for master’s and Ph.D. students in STEM fields.

In 2025, 93 percent of the 635 surveyed institutions responded, including all 187 classified as schools with the highest levels of research spending and Ph.D. production, also known as R1 institutions.

Of those elite research institutions, 132 enrolled fewer new doctoral students in the surveyed fields in 2025 than in 2024.

The Times analyzed trends at these schools, and found that new, full-time Ph.D. enrollments in engineering programs fell by 14 percent. In science and health fields, the collective drop was nearly 11 percent, while mathematics and computer science enrollments together fell by 8 percent.

A previous Times analysis of new Ph.D. enrollments at 27 major research universities in the country found similar trends.

Some fields, like biology and biomedical programs, civil engineering and medical research, were hit especially hard. But no field saw an increase in incoming Ph.D. students.

Source: National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics

In addition to physical and life sciences, such as chemistry and biology, the federal survey also includes data on social sciences like anthropology, economics and sociology. New enrollments in those fields declined by about 10 percent.

The survey’s findings are in line with other data showing a substantial decline in international students choosing to pursue degrees in the United States. New enrollments by doctoral students on temporary visas fell by almost 17 percent at major research universities in the N.S.F. survey, more than twice the rate of declines among citizens and permanent residents.

The drop in the number of foreign students embarking on master’s degrees was even larger, with enrollments declining 28 percent at major research universities. The number of U.S. citizens and permanent residents entering those programs increased by 9 percent.

While most universities saw a decrease in new graduate enrollments, a handful saw a significant rise.

The University of Texas at Austin had one of the largest increases of incoming Ph.D. students, both domestic and international, among all R1 universities. Its mathematics and computer science programs saw enrollment rise from 56 students in 2024 to 94 in 2025. University administrators credited the increase to a dedicated strategy to support growth in federal research funding.

While many universities have seen funding disruptions under the Trump administration and individual researchers have lost grants, some schools have seen increases, often in areas linked to government priorities.

U.T. Austin already had a research portfolio “that really aligns with federal priorities,” said Fernanda Leite, the university’s vice president for research. That includes artificial intelligence, energy, quantum computing and material sciences.

David Vanden Bout, dean of the college of natural sciences at U.T. Austin, said that the university also made a choice not to cut back on Ph.D. admissions despite funding uncertainties and visa restrictions.

“There has been a hope that that would actually give us a competitive advantage,” he said. “Because as other schools cut back on their admissions, we were going to get a greater lion’s share of the really top students.”

Dr. York noted that, while the survey provides a broad snapshot of graduate enrollment trends across the nation, many questions remain, including how the declines impacted students of different socioeconomic backgrounds and where prospective Ph.D. students went instead. He also emphasized that this data only reflects the first year of the second Trump administration.

As more data comes out, he said, it will “illuminate how funding or immigration uncertainties are currently influencing university and student decision making.”
